rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to spread unknown compounds across the window and reveal whether any are strongly retained or elute too early. This gives a balanced first map of retention and selectivity for the 10-component mixture.

All 10 compounds are already baseline-resolved, so the main opportunity is to reduce analysis time without losing the minimum resolution around the 6–8 min cluster. Halving the gradient time keeps chemistry comparable while testing whether CRF improves through a lower time penalty.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the central cluster, especially peaks 5–7. A modest increase to 12 min should selectively recover resolution in that region while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a near-zero time penalty.

Increasing from 10 to 12 min improved the crowded 6/7 pair substantially with no time penalty, so a further small increase is the most direct way to approach full resolution while likely staying in the zero-penalty region. Keeping phi and temperature fixed isolates the gradient-time effect near the current optimum.

The limiting pair continues to improve monotonically as tG increases, and there is still no time penalty, so 16 min is the next logical step toward full resolution and possibly CRF 1.0. This keeps selectivity unchanged and tests whether the crowded mid-run pair crosses the threshold.

At 16 min the resolution term is maxed but a time penalty appears, so improving selectivity rather than stretching the gradient is the better path. A modest temperature decrease may increase retention and differentially open the critical 6/7 pair enough to reach full resolution at 14 min while keeping the run in the no-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity and shifted the critical overlap earlier, so test the opposite direction. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the local selectivity of the crowded middle cluster while keeping the successful 14 min gradient and zero time penalty.

Temperature changes worsened selectivity, so keep T at the best value and instead slightly steepen only the initial part of the gradient by raising phi0. This targets the crowded mid-eluting cluster without greatly affecting the late peak, and may shift relative spacing enough to improve the limiting pair while retaining a zero time penalty.

Raising phi0 improved CRF slightly, and the limiting 6/7 pair still appears gradient-time controlled. Extending to 16 min with the better phi0 setting is the cleanest test of whether full resolution can now be achieved with only a small or possibly acceptable time penalty.

Current performance is nearly ideal, so make a small, local selectivity probe rather than a big change. Slightly lowering phi1 while keeping phi0 and tG fixed may preserve full resolution but pull the late part of the gradient into a more favorable shape, potentially removing the tiny remaining time penalty and reaching CRF 1.0.

Lowering phi1 increased run time, so instead probe whether a slightly higher phi0 can retain the excellent resolution while shortening retention enough to eliminate the small remaining time penalty. This is a minimal change around the current optimum and directly targets CRF 1.0.

Since 0.15/0.95/16/40 reached CRF 1.000, the only useful follow-up is a very local robustness check. Increasing phi0 one step tests whether the optimum sits on a plateau that still preserves full resolution with no time penalty.

The optimum is clearly centered near phi0 0.15, and raising phi0 further reduced the critical 6/7 resolution. A small increase in tG from the winning method tests whether there is a neighboring plateau of full-resolution methods, with only a modest risk of time penalty.

The best point is bracketed in tG: 18 min adds time penalty, so the remaining useful check is whether 14 min with the improved phi0 still keeps the critical pair above threshold and possibly also gives CRF 1.0. This is the most informative local test around the confirmed optimum.

We already have the global maximum at 0.15/0.95/16/40, so only a tiny neighborhood check is justified. Lowering phi1 one step tests method robustness and whether a slightly different terminal strength can maintain full resolution without compromising the zero time penalty.

We are only mapping the local plateau around the optimum now. Lowering phi1 another step checks whether terminal composition can be reduced while retaining full resolution, helping define robustness around the already-achieved CRF maximum.

The composition optimum is well defined, so the only remaining nearby factor to probe is a small temperature increase around the winning method. This checks whether the CRF 1.000 point is a narrow apex or part of a broader robust plateau in selectivity space.

The 45 C test showed temperature strongly perturbs selectivity near the optimum, so a symmetric check at 35 C will complete the local robustness map around the winning method. This confirms whether 40 C is uniquely optimal or whether a cooler condition can also sustain full resolution.

Temperature is clearly suboptimal away from 40 C, so the remaining informative axis is terminal composition. A one-step further decrease in phi1 maps the lower edge of the full-resolution plateau around the optimum and tests robustness while staying close to the best method.

We already found the optimum, so the remaining value is defining its neighborhood. Testing a longer tG at the best phi settings completes the local time-dimension map and confirms that added gradient time only sacrifices CRF through time penalty once full resolution is already achieved.

With the optimum already achieved, the only remaining useful exploration is nearby interaction effects between phi1 and tG. Pairing the shorter 14 min gradient with a lower phi1 tests whether the added retention can recover the critical pair without incurring the stronger time penalty seen at 16 min.

Two different methods now achieve CRF 1.000, suggesting a ridge of equivalent optima. Testing the intermediate phi1 at the same phi0 and tG maps that ridge and checks whether the maximum is robust across terminal composition.

At tG 14 min, phi1 0.85 gives CRF 1.000 while 0.90 falls just short, so testing 0.80 defines the lower side of that optimal ridge. This efficiently maps the robustness window of full-resolution, zero-penalty conditions.

Both 0.15/0.95/16/40 and 0.15/0.85/14/40 achieve CRF 1.000, so a useful last-phase probe is whether the optimal ridge extends to higher phi0 when paired with the shorter, weaker-end gradient. This tests a neighboring composition interaction while staying close to the known optimum region.

The final untested local corner around the second CRF 1.000 method is the lower phi0 side. This completes the nearby composition map and tests whether the full-resolution, zero-penalty ridge extends symmetrically around phi0 0.15.
